newsitem.title: RWANDA: Canadian peace force stuck at Rwanda airport.
newsitem.headline: Canadian peace force stuck at Rwanda airport.

text.p: The Canadian vanguard sent to Rwanda to establish the headquarters of a planned international force for Zaire was prevented from leaving Kigali airport with their weapons on Sunday and threatened to fly out again.
Three Hercules C-130 military transport planes carrying 34 Canadians and equipment landed in the Rwandan capital but a Canadian embassy official said the soldiers were not able to leave the airport.
The official said Rwandan authorities would not let the Canadians move around with weapons because the United Nations -- which authorised the force -- had not arranged clearance.
The embassy official said the Canadians would not leave their equipment unguarded and, "if worst came to worst", they would repack the aircraft and fly out.

The U.N. Security Council on Friday unanimously approved the deployment of the Canadian-led force until March 31 to ensure food and medicine reaches refugees flooding back to Rwanda from Zaire after two years of exile.
Since hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees started flooding back home from Zaire on Friday, Rwanda's government has said the force is no longer needed.

"Our position is that the force was coming to create this corridor for the refugees to come home and now they are coming home. So we don't see any need for the force to come," Rwandan presidential spokesman Joseph Bideri told Reuters.
Major Rod Babuik, head of the Canadian contingent, earlier told Reuters that between 500-700 personnel would be based in Kigali as part of the Canadian-led U.N. multinational intervention force.
"The situation is very fluid, the movement of the refugees has had a big impact on what is happening, but we have just to carry on with our plan which is to 'recce' out sites," he said.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the United States and its allies might modify the plan, but U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien said such a force was still needed in troubled eastern Zaire.

"I can see the need for such a force...Don't think only of what you see on the television screens. There is a huge number of refugees that are absolutely invisible but are still very much in eastern Zaire," Chretien said in a BBC radio interview.
